For \(90 \le n \le 100\), we have \(n+11>100\), so
\[
M(n+11)=n+1.
\]
Thus
\[
M(n)=M(M(n+11))=M(n+1).
\]
Since \(M(101)=91\), this gives
\[
M(90)=M(91)=\cdots=M(100)=M(101)=91.
\]

Now use backward induction. Assume \(M(m)=91\) for all \(m\) with \(n<m\le 100\). For \(n\le 89\), we have \(n+11\le 100\), so by the induction hypothesis \(M(n+11)=91\). Hence
\[
M(n)=M(M(n+11))=M(91)=91.
\]
Therefore \(M(n)=91\) for every positive integer \(n\le 100\).

For \(n>101\), \(M(n)=n-10>91\), so no further solutions exist beyond \(n=101\). Thus the solutions are
\[
1,2,3,\dots,100,101.
\]

So the number of solutions is
\[
\boxed{101}.
\]
